bib.title: Augmenting Language Models with Long-Term Memory

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Augmenting Language Models with Long-Term Memory (LongMem). Weizhi Wang, Li Dong, Hao Cheng, Xiaodong Liu, Xifeng Yan, Jianfeng Gao, Furu Wei (UCSB, Microsoft Research). arXiv:2306.07174v1 [cs.CL], 12 Jun 2023. The PDF says only "arXiv"; no venue is printed (preprint v1). The extraction does not show NeurIPS 2023, so do not assert it.

COVERAGE: All 48,938 chars read, 14 pages, including the abstract, methods, experiments, ablations, related work, conclusion, references (skimmed) and Appendices A-C. The extraction is clean. I did not run the figures script, so figure 4 plot text is garbled. No Limitations section exists.

NOTE ON FIT: This is a model-architecture paper (attention K/V cache plus a trained side-network). It is not about agent or application memory (summaries, stores, MemGPT-style). Check how note 06 frames it.

CLAIMS
1. LongMem reaches 40.5% suffix-identification accuracy on ChapterBreak AO3 (ctx-8k), above GPT-3 (28%) and sparse-attention baselines.
 number: 40.5% (ctx-8k); 37.7% (4k); 39.4% (6k); GPT-3 28%; GPT-2* 18.4%; MemTRM 28.3/28.7/28.7
 setup: Zero-shot, AO3 subset. The model is a reproduced GPT-2 407M backbone (LongMem total 558M) with 1k local context. The 4k/6k/8k prefix is loaded into cached memory. Candidate suffixes are scored by perplexity. The GPT-3 and x-former baselines are cited from Sun et al. (STI22), not rerun.
 quote: "LONG MEM 558M 1K ∞ 37.7% 39.4% 40.5%" and "achieves the state-of-the-art performance of 40.5% accuracy on ChapterBreakAO3 suffix identification benchmark and outperforms both the strong long-context transformers and latest LLM GPT-3 with 313x larger parameters."
 where: Table 3 and Sec 3.2, p.8

2. Long-text perplexity improves by 1.38 to 1.62 on PG-22 splits and by 1.0 on ArXiv, against the GPT-2* baseline.
 number: PG-22 S1-S5: GPT-2* 22.78/24.39/24.12/24.97/18.07 vs LongMem 21.29/23.01/22.55/23.35/16.71; ArXiv 11.05 vs 10.05; MemTRM 21.77/23.56/23.23/24.16/17.39 and ArXiv 10.81
 setup: Zero-shot token-level PPL. In-context length 1k, in-memory length 65k. GPT-2* has no memory. PG-22 is Project Gutenberg books from 2020-2022, and ArXiv is the Pile's ArXiv subset (out of distribution).
 quote: "LONG MEM 1k 65k 21.29 23.01 22.55 23.35 16.71 10.05" and "with improvements of -1.38 to -1.62 perplexity on different length splits of PG-22, and -1.0 ppl on ARXIV datasets."
 where: Table 2, p.7-8. Note the PG-22 S5 split (>1M tokens) has a single document.

3. Memory-augmented in-context learning with 2000 extra demonstrations in memory gives +8.0 average accuracy at 20-shot, with large per-task gains.
 number: 20-shot avg: GPT-2* 58.7, MemTRM 58.6, LongMem 66.7; 4-shot avg: 55.6, 55.6, 58.4; SST-2 20-shot 68.2 vs 78.0; SQuAD 3-shot EM 22.28 vs 26.77 (+4.5)
 setup: 5 NLU datasets (SST-2, MR, Subj, SST-5, MPQA). 2000 extra demos are cached in memory, and 6 seeds are averaged. Chunk size 2 was selected on the SST-2 validation set. SQuAD uses 200 extra demos in memory and greedy decoding. Per-task standard deviations are large (up to about 14).
 quote: "LONG MEM achieves remarkable improvements on all NLU tasks in 20-shot sufficient in-context setting, with +8.0 average scores increase over pretrained GPT-2* and MemTRM." and "+4.5 EM score increase on SQuAD."
 where: Tables 4-5, Sec 3.3, p.8-9

4. The decoupled design (frozen backbone as memory encoder, trainable SideNet as retriever and reader) is claimed to avoid memory staleness, which the coupled MemTRM suffers from. Staleness is the stated motivation, and the paper has no isolated staleness experiment. LongMem beats MemTRM under identical token budget and hyperparameters on every table.
 number: none
 setup: MemTRM was reproduced and trained on the same 26B tokens.
 quote: "as the model parameters are updated, cached older representations in memory may have distributional shifts from those from the latest model, thereby limiting the effectiveness of the memory augmentation."
 where: Intro, p.2

5. Efficiency: with a 1k local context plus memory, LongMem runs faster and uses far less GPU memory than dense attention at the same effective length.
 number: 4k effective: 22638 vs 14666 tokens/s, 13335 vs 20671 MB; 8k effective: 21343 vs 8417 tokens/s, 13437 vs 54195 MB
 setup: GPT-2* dense attention at 4k/8k vs LongMem with 1k in-context and 3k/7k in-memory.
 quote: "LONG MEM 1k 7k 21343 13437" and "GPT-2* 8k N/A 8417 54195"
 where: Table 6, App. A, p.13

6. Retrieval overhead is modest.
 number: 15 ms per 1k tokens, which is 55% of the backbone forward-pass time
 setup: faiss exact-search index on GPU, per-GPU memory bank of 65,536 key-value pairs, chunk size 4, K=64 (16 chunks).
 quote: "The retrieval takes about 15ms per 1k tokens, which is 55% timecost of backbone LLM forwarding pass."
 where: Sec 3.1, p.6

7. Chunk size matters for fine-grained tasks. Chunk size 2 was best for ICL, per the paper (SST-2 72/78/77.8 for csz 1/2/4 as read from the Figure 4a text, which is garbled). Token-to-chunk retrieval (mean-pooled keys, top K/csz chunks) shrinks the index and is said to improve accuracy.
 number: csz in {2,4,8} per text; the figure legend shows csz=1/2/4, an internal inconsistency.
 quote: "The chunk size of 2 yields the best performance on in-context learning tasks on five NLU datasets"
 where: Sec 3.4, Fig 4a, p.9-10

8. Memory size should match the document length. A 16k memory beat 65k for books averaging 8k-50k tokens.
 number: 16k best; tested {8k, 16k, 32k, 65k}
 setup: Inference-time ablation on PG-22. The training memory size was 65k.
 quote: "To model the books with average 8k-50k length, the smaller memory size 16k which is consistent with the average length of target books yields the best perplexity."
 where: Sec 3.4, p.9

9. Mechanism. The frozen LLM caches attention K/V from layer 18 of 24 per segment into a FIFO bank of the latest M=65k tokens. The SideNet has 12 layers (151M params) initialised from the backbone and uses cross-network residuals. Memory fusion is a gated joint-attention layer at SideNet layer 9. Adaptation trains on 26B tokens with a 1024-token sequence.
 quote: "Hl = sigmoid(g) · A + (1 − sigmoid(g)) · M" and "the memory bank removes the key-value pairs of the oldest sequences and appends the current sequences"
 where: Sec 2, p.4-6

LIMITS
- Small-scale evidence: a reproduced GPT-2 407M with Alibi, trained on a Pile subset. It was never tested on modern instruction-tuned LLMs.
- Requires adapter training (26B tokens on 16 V100s) and a white-box model whose attention K/V can be read. It does not work with API-only models.
- The memory holds raw K/V vectors, not text, so it cannot be inspected or edited.
- The memory is a FIFO queue of the latest M previous inputs. It is not an unbounded store, despite the "unlimited-length" wording.
- No downstream agent, dialogue or QA-over-memory evaluation beyond SQuAD, where the extra demos are task training examples.
- ICL gains have high variance across seeds (SD up to about 14 points). The ICL setup is classification with label tokens, a favourable case for retrieval.
- Hyperparameters (csz) were selected on SST-2 validation.
- ChapterBreak comparisons mix numbers cited from other papers with the authors' own runs.
- The paper has no limitations section.
- The 2023 dating predates long-context models of 128k and more.

BUILDS ON: Memorizing Transformer (Wu, Rabe, Hutchins, Szegedy; [WRHS22]), which supplies the kNN joint attention and is the staleness baseline; Side-Tuning (Zhang et al. 2020); Transformer-XL (Dai et al. 2019); Sun et al. ChapterBreak [STI22]; RETRO (Borgeaud et al. 2021) and Lv et al. 2023, cited for chunk retrieval; Alibi (Press 2021); faiss (Johnson 2021); the Pile (Gao 2020); PG-19 (Rae et al. 2019, as [RPJL19]).

CODE: none in the paper (code is at https://aka.ms/LongMem). Key equation: "HlSide = fΘlSide(Hl−1Side) + (H2lLLM − H2l−2LLM )" (eq. 1, p.5).

FIGURES (I did not run the captions script; the captions below are from the extracted text)
- Fig 1, p.2: caching and retrieval flow, with the frozen LLM writing K/V to the bank and the SideNet reading the top-k.
- Fig 2, p.3: architecture with the frozen and trainable layers.
- Fig 3, p.6: batching so that consecutive segments of a document land in consecutive batches.
- Fig 4, p.10: (a) accuracy on 5 NLU tasks by chunk size; (b) delta perplexity on PG-22 by memory size.
Fig 1 explains the design fastest.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The Fig 4 text is garbled (the (b) axis is unreadable, and the legend csz=1/2/4 conflicts with the text's {2,4,8}). Table 5 subscript std values are partly run together (e.g. "68.3 11.6" means 68.3 with SD 11.6). The text has a typo, "msz of 65 tokens", which should read 65k. Appendix labelling is off: the text cites "Appendix C" for training details, but they are in section B. The venue is not printed.
